name: PL/pgSQL
title: PL/pgSQL (PostgreSQL 18)
lifecycleNote: PostgreSQL 18; PL/pgSQL ships with the engine, so the language release is the database release.

type.text: **Static typing over SQL data types**: Every variable, parameter, and return value declares a type, and a body that violates its declarations fails when the function is compiled
**`%TYPE` and `%ROWTYPE` anchor a declaration to the schema**: `emp%ROWTYPE` follows the table's column list, so a column change does not require editing the declaration
**Polymorphic parameters keep one algorithm generic**: `anyelement` and `anyarray` let a single function run over many types, with the type fixed per call

**Operators resolve by operand type (T8)**: `+`, `||`, and `&&` name different operations for different types, and `CREATE OPERATOR` lets an extension add meanings, so an expression's sense follows from the operand types
**A `record` variable defers its row type to run time**: The row shape is known only when a value is assigned, so a mistyped field surfaces on the path that reaches it
**NULL is the default value and it propagates (T10)**: A declared variable starts as NULL, three-valued logic applies, so `IF x = 5` is not true when `x` is NULL
**A signature says what a function returns, not what it does (T12)**: A function that mutates tables, reads a foreign table, or sends notifications looks like any other function

construction.text: **A function is a closed unit**: Local variables are private to the call, and the signature is the whole interface, so a caller cannot reach inside
**`CREATE FUNCTION` and `CREATE PROCEDURE` compile at creation**: The body is checked once when it is deployed, and a caller binds to the name and the signature
**Anonymous `DO` blocks run ad-hoc logic without a deployment step**: A one-off migration or maintenance script is a block, not a schema object
**Triggers fire implicitly**: A trigger function runs in response to a data change, so the writer of a statement cannot see from the statement which code will run
**`SECURITY DEFINER` is decided in the definition, not at the call**: A caller sees only a function name; whether it runs with the owner's rights follows from the definition

memory.text: **No manual memory management**: The PostgreSQL server owns process memory, and a block never names an address or frees a byte
**The server sizes the work areas**: A sort or a hash inside a function's statements gets its memory from `work_mem`, which is a setting, not a statement property
**`RETURN QUERY` materialises its result before returning**: A set-returning function builds its whole output in a tuplestore, so the call's memory follows the result size
**A `CREATE TEMP TABLE` inside a function outlives the call**: The table persists for the session, so a local act leaves a session-scoped resource behind

error.text: **The block separates the normal path from the recovery path**: `BEGIN ... EXCEPTION WHEN unique_violation THEN ...` gives a named handler section, and conditions match by code or by name
**`RAISE EXCEPTION` carries a code and a detail**: `RAISE EXCEPTION 'msg' USING ERRCODE = '23505'` raises a failure a caller's handler can match on
**`GET STACKED DIAGNOSTICS` reports the caught error**: A handler can read the error's code, message, constraint, context, and line
**A handler can swallow (Er3)**: An `EXCEPTION` block that catches and returns normally lets the caller see success, and `WHEN OTHERS` is the widest net
**A failure cannot travel as a value (Er4)**: The failure path is the exception path, so a fallible operation cannot be folded into an expression or returned as a result the caller inspects

concurrency.text: **A procedure can manage its own transaction**: A `CALL`ed procedure may `COMMIT` and `ROLLBACK` (since PostgreSQL 11), while a function always runs inside its caller's transaction
**`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` names the rows to lock in the query text**: The lock is declared by the statement rather than by a separate call
**Advisory locks give an explicit lock service**: `pg_advisory_lock` serialises an application-level critical section across sessions under a declared key
**Session state is shared by default (K2)**: Custom session parameters set with `set_config`, session temp tables, and `current_setting` are visible to every function that runs in the session

**Transaction isolation and declared locks do not order independent work**: Two sessions' multi-step work is ordered only by the locks its statements name, so any ordering the source relies on is an agreement no declaration carries

platform.text: **Cannot function outside one engine (P1)**: A PL/pgSQL program needs PostgreSQL or a compatible fork, so the unit of deployment is a database schema
**Portability is the engine's, not the artifact's (Y10)**: The program runs wherever its PostgreSQL release runs, and the language has no build target of its own
**Managed services track the engine's calendar**: A managed PostgreSQL carries the PL/pgSQL of its engine version, so the available surface follows the provider's upgrade
**Foreign languages load in-process (T14)**: `LANGUAGE C` and the untrusted PLs such as `plpython3u` run outside PL/pgSQL's checks, so a boundary no signature can see separates the two sides
**Client interfaces are standard**: libpq, ODBC, and JDBC reach the engine, so a client is not bound to one binary protocol

performance.text: **Statements inside a function use cached plans**: A function's static SQL is planned once per session and reused, so a call does not re-parse
**Set-based statements in the body do the heavy lifting**: One `INSERT ... SELECT` inside the function carries the optimiser's plan, so the procedural wrapper is not the hot path
**Row-by-row loops pay per-row context switches**: A loop that fetches one row at a time runs far slower than its set-based equivalent
**A plan regression arrives hidden inside the call**: A caller cannot see the queries inside a function, so a changed plan surfaces as the function being slow

ecosystem.text: **The extension ecosystem supplies the libraries**: `CREATE EXTENSION` loads packaged capabilities such as PostGIS, pg_trgm, and pgcrypto into the database
**PGXN catalogs shareable extensions**: A public registry indexes community extensions with releases and metadata
**PostgreSQL's popularity carries the market**: Documentation, books, courses, and hiring are abundant
**The stack is open and permissively licensed**: The engine, the client tools, and the documentation carry no per-seat licence
**Tooling centres on the engine's own tools**: psql, pg_dump, and pgAdmin cover administration and query work, and the procedural language has no dedicated environment of its own

evolution.text: **Major releases keep the language**: A PL/pgSQL function written years ago compiles in the current release
**Deprecation is announced before removal**: The release notes and the documentation mark obsolescent features, so an upgrade is planned rather than discovered
**A feature arrives with the engine's major release**: Adoption follows the server a deployment can upgrade to, not a separate language release
**The community's own decisions govern the change**: No independent standard bounds the syntax, so the release notes are the definition's change log

domain.text: **Excellent fit for data-centric logic**: A function runs beside its tables with SQL directly in the body, so a rule executes where the data is
**A full procedural language inside SQL**: Loops, records, cursors, and subprograms live in the same unit as the queries
**The engine reaches beyond its own schema**: Foreign data wrappers and `dblink` read remote sources, and other PLs run beside PL/pgSQL in the same database
**Domain lock-in (D1)**: The language exists to run inside PostgreSQL, so the PostgreSQL data tier is the only domain
**It is not a runtime for arbitrary programs**: A user interface, a heavy text workload, or a long-running service belongs in another language beside PL/pgSQL

learning.text: **Gentle for a SQL developer**: A block with `DECLARE`, `BEGIN`, and `END` reads like SQL with control flow added
**The documentation is complete and canonical**: The PL/pgSQL chapter of the PostgreSQL manual documents every construct with runnable examples
**`SELECT INTO` is silent on an empty result**: A plain `SELECT INTO` assigns NULL when the query returns no rows, and `STRICT` is the opt-in that makes it error
**Engine behaviour is a separate body of knowledge**: Locks, MVCC, and transaction semantics matter more than syntax for correct code

syntax.text: **Verbose (S1)**: Every unit needs `CREATE FUNCTION`, a dollar-quoted body, and `DECLARE`, `BEGIN`, and `END` sections before it does anything
**Keyword-led and readable**: Statements read as verbs, and the block boundaries are visible in the source
**The body is one dollar-quoted string**: `$$ ... $$` hides the body from the outer statement's parser, so a function deploys as a single statement
**Function overloading hides the signature**: Two functions may share a name and differ by argument types, so a call's target follows from the argument list

testing.text: **No test framework ships with the engine (G1)**: psql and the server tools provide no assertion or runner, so a suite depends on pgTAP or a hand-rolled harness
**pgTAP is the established framework**: An open-source test framework runs database tests with xUnit-style assertion functions
**Transaction control isolates a test**: A test can run inside a transaction that rolls back, leaving the database unchanged
**The engine traces execution**: `RAISE` writes to the server log with line numbers, and `auto_explain` logs the plans of statements inside functions
**A suite needs a server**: Tests run inside the database they exercise, so the harness depends on a PostgreSQL instance and on deployment rights

security.text: **Static SQL in the body is parameterised automatically**: The function's variables become `$n` parameters of the planned statement, so values cannot change the parse
**`GRANT` and roles express least privilege**: `EXECUTE` on a function is granted per role, and the function signature is the grantable interface
**`SECURITY DEFINER` states the effective identity in the definition**: `ALTER FUNCTION ... SECURITY DEFINER` plus a pinned `SET search_path` makes the rights and the environment explicit
**Known vulnerability/injection (Q3)**: `EXECUTE` with a built string turns concatenated input into code, and `format()` with `%I` and `%L` is the mitigation, not a guarantee
**Definer's-rights functions can escalate**: A `SECURITY DEFINER` function runs with its owner's rights, so it needs a pinned search path and an audit

tradeoffs: **Logic beside the data is deliberate**: A rule that runs beside its tables is enforced for every writer; the cost is that the rule sits outside the application's test suite and profilers

**A session cache in custom parameters is deliberate**: `set_config` keeps a value for the session without a table; the cost is staleness, since nothing invalidates the value when the underlying data changes

**Dynamic SQL is deliberate for DDL and for a flexible filter**: `EXECUTE` with `format()` reaches names a static statement cannot; the cost is the plan, since a built string is parsed and planned on every execution
**`SECURITY DEFINER` is deliberate for gated access**: It exposes one narrow operation instead of table grants; the cost is an audit duty, since the function runs with its owner's rights
verdict: PL/pgSQL's coupling is set by its host engine and governed by its community. Functions are closed units with typed declarations, the `EXCEPTION ... WHEN` section gives a structured failure path, static SQL in the body is parameterised automatically, and the extension registry, the open licence, and community governance give this shelf's most open ecosystem. Main strengths: open source end to end, an independent steward, complete documentation, automatic parameterisation, and real modularity at function granularity. Main weaknesses: everything runs inside PostgreSQL, NULL starts in every declared variable and propagates, signatures carry no effects, dynamic SQL turns built strings into code, a handler can swallow a failure and return success, `RETURN QUERY` materialises its result, and the block structure adds boilerplate to every unit.

energy.text: Runs inside a database engine: energy and time are the engine's, not the program's.

ai-readiness.text: Procedural SQL is thin in model training data relative to mainstream languages, so generated PL/pgSQL mixes in other dialects' syntax [@joel2025lowresource].

safety.text: No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

delivery.note: The database stores the source text and parses it; no compiled unit crosses a boundary
